title: Growing holy
hook: grace keeps growing a person; John Wesley even spoke of being made perfect in love

segments.voice: Yesterday, assurance: a confident trust for some churches, a humble hope for others. Your line was trust, not fear. Where did trust interrupt the worry? Day one thousand ninety-two.

"But grow in grace." Those words sit near the very end of the second letter of Peter, and they take something for granted. The people reading the letter already belong to God. And they're still unfinished. A kid who knows she's loved at home still has to learn to share the last cookie, to say sorry first, to tell the truth when a lie would be quicker. Being loved doesn't end the growing. It's where the growing starts. Christians have a long word for that slow change. And an English preacher named John Wesley, whose followers became the Methodists, pushed it a long way: he spoke of a heart made perfect in love. Today's word: sanctification.

Start with the word holy. In the Bible, holy often means set apart, belonging to God, the way a cup set aside for the altar is no longer just a kitchen cup. Paul writes to the Thessalonians, in the King James: "For this is the will of God, even your sanctification." So sanctification is two things at once. You're set apart. And then, slowly, you become what you were set apart for. The churches describe that growth with different pictures. Lutheran and Reformed Christians, as we saw a few days back, speak of being declared right with God by faith; being made holy is the lifelong work that follows, and in their teaching it isn't finished this side of death. Catholics speak of grace that heals and lifts, growing in a person through the sacraments and through their free cooperation. The Orthodox word, theosis, pictures the whole journey as being drawn into God's own life. Then Wesley. He read Jesus's words in the Sermon on the Mount, "Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect," and he asked a plain question: would God command what could never happen? His answer was what he called Christian perfection. He didn't mean a life with no mistakes. In his own account, people made perfect in love still misjudge things and still need forgiveness. He meant a heart so full of love for God and neighbor that love runs the whole house, with no rooms kept back. Methodist and Holiness churches have taught a version of this. Other Christians think it promises too much for this life. Wesley leaned on a line from John's first letter we heard yesterday: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear." He heard a promise in it for this life. Notice where that leaves yesterday's line. Trust comes first. Then love has room to grow.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: grow one small habit of love. Settle, and let your breathing slow down. Bring to mind one person you'll see today or tomorrow. Now choose one small thing you could do for them again and again. A real hello instead of a nod. Letting them finish a sentence. A message that asks how they're actually doing. Keep it small enough to repeat. Growth, in this picture, is less a leap than a habit watered daily. If you pray, you can ask for grace to keep at it. If you don't, simply hold the person and the habit together for a while. The bell holds the time.
Sanctification. Being made holy: set apart for God, then grown, slowly, into love.
Your line: perfect in love. Today, do your small habit once, on purpose, and notice if it comes easier the next time. Day one thousand ninety-two.

howItsDone: Christians in many churches speak of sanctification as lifelong growth in holiness through prayer, scripture, worship and the sacraments; Methodist and Holiness churches also teach Wesley's hope of a heart made perfect in love.

myth: Wesley's perfection meant a life with no mistakes
he meant a heart full of love for God and neighbor; in his account, such people still misjudge things and still need forgiveness.
Paul calls sanctification the will of God
"for this is the will of God, even your sanctification" (1 Thessalonians 4:3).
every church agrees holiness can be complete in this life
Methodist and Holiness churches have taught a version of it; Lutheran and Reformed teaching says the work isn't finished this side of death.

fork.setup: you're John Wesley, reading "be ye therefore perfect." what do you make of it?
options: an impossible ideal, meant only to humble us.
God commands it, so love can truly fill a heart.
a rule for monks and nuns, not ordinary people.
fork.reveal: Wesley asked whether God would command the impossible, and taught Christian perfection: not flawlessness, but a heart run by love.

original.note: Greek: sanctification, making holy — the word Paul uses in 1 Thessalonians 4:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: sanctification means being perfect and never messing up.
what it means: being set apart for God, then slowly grown into love. churches picture the growth differently.
what a scholar hears: hagiasmos is Paul's word in 1 Thessalonians 4:3. Wesley's "Christian perfection" was perfection in love, not freedom from error.
